Tentu! Berdasarkan Master Plan kamu, berikut **Draft Introduction** untuk paper berjudul:

> *"Effect of Cement Treated Base Thickness on Mechanical Responses of Asphalt Surface Course under Combined Traffic-Thermal Loading: A Finite Element Study Using ABAQUS"*

---

## 1. INTRODUCTION (DRAFT)

Flexible pavement structures in tropical regions such as Indonesia are subjected to two dominant loading mechanisms: repetitive traffic loads and daily thermal cycles. The asphalt surface course, being the uppermost layer, directly experiences both mechanical stresses from wheel loads and thermally induced strains from ambient temperature fluctuations. These combined effects can accelerate distresses such as fatigue cracking, rutting, and thermal cracking, ultimately reducing pavement service life [1–3].

To enhance the structural capacity of flexible pavements, cement-treated base (CTB) layers have been widely adopted as a cost-effective alternative to granular bases. CTB—a mixture of aggregate, cement, and water—offers improved stiffness, load distribution capability, and resistance to permanent deformation compared to conventional unbound granular materials [4,5]. Previous studies have established that increasing CTB thickness generally reduces tensile strains at the bottom of the asphalt layer, thereby mitigating fatigue damage [6,7]. However, the majority of these studies have focused solely on traffic-induced mechanical responses, neglecting the contribution of thermal loading—a significant factor in tropical climates where pavement surface temperatures can vary by 20–30°C diurnally.

Furthermore, while extensive research has been conducted on CTB thicknesses ranging from 100 to 200 mm for low- to medium-volume roads [8,9], limited attention has been given to the range of **200–300 mm** specifically for heavy-traffic highways, and even fewer studies have systematically examined how variations within this range affect the *surface course*—the most critical layer from a maintenance perspective.

The mechanical behavior of asphalt concrete under combined loading is complex: asphalt exhibits viscoelastic properties that are highly temperature- and rate-dependent, while CTB behaves as a quasi-brittle cementitious material susceptible to micro-cracking under tensile stresses induced by thermal gradients [10,11]. Capturing the interaction between these two distinct material behaviors under simultaneous traffic and thermal loading requires a robust numerical approach. The **finite element method (FEM) using ABAQUS** provides the capability to model viscoelastic asphalt response, concrete damaged plasticity (CDP) for the cement-treated base, and the coupled mechanical–thermal boundary conditions necessary to simulate realistic field conditions [12,13].

The present study aims to investigate the **effect of CTB thickness on the mechanical responses of the asphalt surface course (AC-WC)** under combined traffic and thermal loading using three-dimensional finite element modeling. Three CTB thicknesses—**200 mm, 250 mm, and 300 mm**—are analyzed comparatively. The key response parameters evaluated include vertical displacement, horizontal tensile stress, and strain distributions within the surface course. The novelty of this work lies in: (1) a focused analysis of the 200–300 mm CTB thickness range specifically addressing surface course responses—an area underexplored in existing literature; (2) a detailed comparative evaluation of displacement, stress, and strain outputs to identify an optimal CTB thickness based on mechanical criteria; and (3) the incorporation of coupled traffic–thermal loading within a viscoelastic–CDP finite element framework, which represents a more realistic simulation than conventional elastic-layered approaches.

It is hypothesized that **increasing CTB thickness will reduce tensile stresses in the surface course**, with the rate of reduction diminishing beyond a certain threshold—suggesting the existence of an optimal thickness beyond which additional cement-treated material yields marginal mechanical benefit.
